top_stories.title: Voter backlash against AI data centers sweeps midterm elections
points: 30+ local measures restricting data centers passed nationwide, including all 41 local ballot measures tracked by one analysis — a complete narrative defeat for AI companies.
76% of voters in exit polls said they would not want a data center in their own community; 61% disliked candidates who supported local data center construction.
Democrats swept House and Senate with an 11-point swing, with data centers framed as a proxy for 'tech oligarchy' benefiting billionaires at public expense amid cost-of-living anger.

Ohio's Sherrod Brown won his Senate seat after centering his campaign on blocking data centers; the state has 46 planned projects totaling 16 gigawatts (a gigawatt is enough power for roughly 750,000 homes), including Meta's Prometheus and OpenAI's 10-gigawatt Pike County campus.

Texas elected Gina Hinojosa as its first Latina governor on a platform to pause data centers until rules are written; the state has 470 gigawatts of pending proposals — about three times its current grid capacity.

Other winning candidates built platforms partly around data centers: Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed (first Muslim U.S. senator) linked them to surveillance and AI warfare; Georgia's Jon Ossoff attacked $70 billion in claimed data center subsidies as oligarchy.
Despite the backlash, demand for the underlying technology keeps growing: ChatGPT now has 1.2 billion weekly users and 250 million using its voice features, all needing data center capacity to run.

Federal AI policy is still expected to stay incremental rather than sweeping — think whistleblower protections, mandatory pre-release testing of frontier models, and incident reporting — since Trump has pledged to veto aggressive restrictions.

unique_angles.point: Industry spent tens of millions trying to defeat Sherrod Brown; SB 1047 author Scott Wiener also won his San Francisco congressional race, boosting AI-safety advocates in Congress.
NBC exit polls ranked data centers behind cost-of-living (89%) and government corruption (90%) in importance, but ahead of most other issues, at 56% calling them a crucial or major factor.
Local anger reached the point of a recall: one Ohio town recalled its mayor and two commissioners for backing a Meta data center facility.

items.title: Companies grapple with accountability for autonomous AI agents
points: Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code and GitHub's AI coding tools to engineers and quants by October, after praising them in July, frustrating traders who had used them for monitoring and reporting.
Deloitte survey of 3,500 leaders found 40% allow AI to make decisions without human approval, but 23% say accountability for bad outcomes is unclear.
CrowdStrike and Salesforce both launched 'AI Kill Switches' to cut off rogue agents (AI systems that act autonomously) and prevent relaunch, but stopping an agent doesn't undo damage already done.
Wells Fargo's new terms (effective Nov. 24) make customers liable for mistakes or unauthorized acts by their AI agents, placing the burden of proof on customers to show they revoked access.
Apple's annual report warns AI agents may act without permission, resist instructions, or conceal information with irreversible consequences.

items.title: AI agents still struggle with real-world professional tasks
points: SemiAnalysis's GDPx benchmark tested AI across 206 professional tasks in 11 fields (chip design, biology, finance, law); the best performer, Claude Opus 5.5, scored only 12%, followed by Gemini 4 Carbon (10.9%) and GPT-6 Astra (9.6%).
DoorDash's CEO said third-party AI agents placed 'maybe several hundred' orders total, compared to millions of deliveries DoorDash handles daily — minimal real-world adoption.
OpenAI reports ChatGPT search-like queries run at roughly one-fifth of Google's search volume; Google is cutting off Search entirely for schools that disable AI features for student accounts.

items.title: Capturing 'tribal knowledge' before employees leave
points: Only 32% of HR professionals document cultural norms and 43% document client relationships (versus 83% documenting policies), leaving AI assistants to guess at real business rules and give wrong answers.

Tenex Media's five-step process: connect to where knowledge lives (chat, docs, meetings), hunt for informal traces (repeated questions, exceptions), have AI interview knowledge holders, source every claim, and capture knowledge as work happens.

SHRM survey found 'botsitting' (overseeing and correcting AI output) takes managers at least 3 hours weekly per 41% of respondents, and 60% of new-hire trainers say overseeing AI takes as much effort as training a person.

items.title: Verification is the key lever for getting trustworthy AI output
points: Andrej Karpathy noted AI capability peaks in domains that are 'digital, verifiable, and economically valuable' — meaning the AI can test whether its own work actually succeeded.
Claude Code creator Boris Cherny says giving AI a verification feedback loop can '2-3x the quality of the final result'; without it, AI stops when work 'looks done,' not when it 'is done.'

Three practical check types: 'Count It' (objective numeric rules like word or budget limits), 'Look It Up' (AI verifies facts against cited sources), and 'Try It' (AI actually uses the output like a human, e.g., clicking buttons to confirm they work).

Verification is only as reliable as the rules you write — undocumented requirements go unchecked — and SpaceX engineer Lauren Tan cautions that even verification 'is just approximation and can still be wrong.'
Best practice: frame AI prompts around desired outcomes rather than step-by-step instructions, giving the model freedom to find better paths to the goal.

issues.subject: 🤖 Grades vs. Checks: Getting AI Work You Can Trust

headlines: Verification is the hidden lever separating AI users who get overnight results from those stuck prompting all day—AI works best when it can check its own work against clear rules.
Three types of checks unlock 2-3x quality improvement: count-based rules (word limits, budgets), fact-checking via sources, and functional testing (clicking buttons to confirm they work).
Without verification, AI guesses when it's done and stops too early; with it, you can hand a frontier model a goal and let it iterate unsupervised until the outcome meets your criteria.
The gap between 'looks done' and 'is done' is where AI fails—unless you give the model explicit rules to verify success, you become the quality-control bottleneck.

sections.title: Why Verification Changes Everything
points: Andrej Karpathy noted that capability peaks in 'digital, verifiable and economically valuable' domains—verifiable means the AI can test whether its work actually succeeded.

Claude Code creator Boris Cherny stated verification can '2-3x the quality of the final result' by giving the model a feedback loop; without it, AI stops when work 'looks done,' not when it 'is done.'
Agentic engineers scale productivity by building verification systems that let AI iterate for hours unsupervised; the model only stops when it confirms the goal is achieved, not by guessing.

sections.title: Three Actionable Check Types
points: Count It: Rules with one right answer ('under 150 words,' 'under $500 per person,' 'nothing before 10am Saturday') that you can verify yourself in seconds—most reliable because no judgment required.
Look It Up: AI confirms facts by checking secondary sources (vendor pricing pages, PDFs, docs) and cites exact page references; forces the model to anchor claims to reality.
Try It: AI uses the output like a real person would—opening a browser, clicking buttons, testing UI—and iterates until it works; only method that catches whether a button link actually functions.

sections.title: Verification's Limits and Best Practices
points: Verification is only as good as the rules you write; if you don't document a requirement as a check, nothing catches it—especially risky when working outside your expertise.
SpaceX engineer Lauren Tan cautioned verification 'is just approximation and can still be wrong,' but even imperfect checks reduce time spent double-checking agent outputs.
Frame prompts around desired outcomes, not step-by-step instructions—tell the model the destination, not turn-by-turn directions, so it avoids bottlenecks and has freedom to find better paths.

issues.subject: How the Midterm Results Change AI

headlines: Democrats won a decisive 11-point swing in midterms, taking House and Senate, but the real issue driving votes was anger over data center buildouts—61% of voters dislike candidates supporting local data centers—not AI technology itself.

Ohio's Sherrod Brown returned to Senate with mandate to block data centers after making them centerpiece of campaign; state has 46 planned projects totaling 16 gigawatts including Meta's Prometheus and OpenAI's 10-gigawatt Pike County campus.

Texas elected Gina Hinojosa as first Latina governor on platform to moratorium data centers until rules written; state has 470 gigawatts of pending proposals, roughly three times current grid capacity.
All 41 local data center ballot measures passed, signaling complete narrative defeat for AI companies and voter demand for strict rules governing the buildout.

Washington will pursue incremental rules (whistleblower protections, pre-release testing, incident reporting) rather than sweeping restrictions like federal moratorium, as Trump pledges veto power over aggressive Democratic proposals.

sections.title: 1. Data Centers Became the Proxy for Tech Oligarchy and Cost of Living
points: Only 44% of voters ranked AI as very important; economy (84%) and government corruption (90%) dominated, but 61% disliked candidates supporting local data center construction.
Democrats framed data centers as benefiting billionaires while extracting public resources; Republicans constrained by Trump's industry support, couldn't effectively counter the narrative.
NBC exit polls showed 56% called data centers crucial or major factor, placing it behind cost-of-living (89%) and corruption (90%) but ahead of most other hot-button issues.

sections.title: 2. New Democratic Senators Built Platforms Around Blocking Data Centers
points: Sherrod Brown (Ohio) won 18-year Senate veteran seat with data centers as centerpiece, running ads featuring only the sound of a data center hum; industry spent tens of millions to stop him.

Abdul El-Sayed (Michigan), first Muslim U.S. senator, connected data centers, surveillance cameras (Flock cameras), and AI-powered warfare as one dystopian state oppression picture; ran on job loss and bioweapons risks.
Jon Ossoff (Georgia) framed data center subsidies ($70 billion claimed in One Big Beautiful Bill) as symbol of oligarchy; cruised to second term over Trump-backed opponent.

sections.title: 3. Local Voters Decisively Rejected Data Center Expansion
points: All 41 local ballot measures restricting or regulating data centers passed, with Brad Carson calling it an "AI earthquake" signaling complete loss of narrative war by AI companies.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Georgia all elected governors or senators pledging moratoriums or strict rules; nine of ten largest states now run by Democrats, giving states outsized power over buildout.

Scott Wiener, author of California's AI safety bill (SB 1047), won San Francisco congressional race with commanding lead, positioning himself as champion for existential-risk safety advocates over industry allies.

sections.title: 4. Federal AI Policy Likely Incremental, Not Sweeping
points: Trump's promised veto power means no comprehensive federal framework, no national data center moratorium, no restrictions on frontier model training techniques.

Likely wins are cross-party items: whistleblower protections for lab employees, mandatory pre-release testing of frontier models (evaluating capabilities before public release), incident reporting, stronger developer liability, possibly data sovereignty rules (restrictions on where training data can be processed).

Export controls will tangle with debates over pausing, pacing, or prohibiting recursive self-improvement (models improving themselves iteratively); expect hearings with limited practical impact unless Democrats target Elon Musk.
